strengths: Addresses an interesting and timely problem: improving text-to-motion generation for complex, compositional, and out-of-distribution prompts using explicit planning and RL-style optimization.
The proposed pipeline is conceptually coherent, combining a motion tokenizer, LLM-based Chain-of-Thought action planning, supervised cold start, and GRPO-based refinement.
HumanML3D results show competitive performance, with improvements on R-Precision@2/3, MM-Dist, and Diversity relative to several strong baselines.
The ablation study supports that combining CoT with semantic and motion rewards is better than using individual components alone.
weaknesses: The empirical support is substantially incomplete. The paper claims evaluation on multiple benchmarks including KIT-ML, but only HumanML3D quantitative results are shown in the main manuscript.

The claimed gains are modest and mixed: R-Precision@1 is tied with existing methods, FID is worse than several baselines, and MModality is not state of the art. This weakens the claim of broad state-of-the-art performance.

The out-of-distribution and complex-prompt evaluation is almost entirely qualitative, with only a few selected visual examples and no systematic human study, OOD benchmark, or quantitative compositionality metric.

Novelty is limited: the framework largely combines existing ingredients, namely VQ-VAE motion tokenization, LLM-generated rationales, SFT, and GRPO-style RL. The paper does not clearly establish why CoT reasoning is necessary beyond acting as an additional generated plan.

The RL formulation is under-specified. Important details such as group size, sampling strategy, reward weighting or ranking procedure, KL coefficient, training schedule, and stability diagnostics are missing.

The MotionCoT Data Engine is not sufficiently reproducible: the LLM prompt, filtering criteria, regeneration procedure, dataset size after filtering, and quality-control thresholds are not provided in the main paper.

There is a potential mismatch between generated CoT plans and actual motion data: CoTs are produced from captions by an LLM and may hallucinate sub-actions not present in the paired motion, but this risk is not measured or mitigated convincingly.
The paper uses automatic metrics derived from pretrained text-motion encoders that are also used in reward design, raising concerns about reward-metric overfitting and circular evaluation.
Some statements are internally inconsistent or imprecise, e.g. saying GRPO does not rely on explicit reward functions while later defining several explicit rewards.
The comparison and terminology around MotionAgent/MotionLLM are confusing, and the paper claims improvements over MotionAgent while the table labels the baseline as MotionLLM.

strengths: The paper targets an interesting and timely direction: combining language-model reasoning traces with text-to-motion generation, especially for compositional or abstract prompts.
The overall framework is easy to understand at a high level, and the use of a VQ-VAE motion tokenizer plus an LLM backbone is a plausible design choice consistent with recent motion-language work.
The paper includes standard HumanML3D metrics and compares against several relevant baselines, including MoMask, MotionGPT, MotionGPT-2, and MotionLLM/MotionAgent-like methods.
The ablation attempts to separate the effects of CoT supervision, semantic reward, and motion similarity reward, which is the right kind of analysis for the proposed components.
weaknesses: The main claims are substantially stronger than the evidence. The paper repeatedly claims evaluation on multiple benchmarks, including KIT-ML, but only reports quantitative results on HumanML3D. This is a major empirical gap.

Novelty is limited. The core recipe is LLM-generated CoT annotations plus supervised fine-tuning plus GRPO-style RL with existing motion-language rewards. The paper does not convincingly establish a new technical contribution beyond adapting recent LLM reasoning/RL ideas to text-to-motion.

The evaluation is weak for the claimed OOD and compositional reasoning benefits. The evidence for complex and abstract prompts is almost entirely qualitative, with only a few cherry-picked visual examples and no quantitative OOD benchmark, human study, or systematic compositional evaluation.

Reported improvements are modest and mixed. Motion-R1 is not clearly state-of-the-art across metrics: for example, it is worse than MoMask on FID and only ties or slightly improves some R-Precision metrics. The paper nevertheless frames the result as broadly superior.

The RL formulation is under-specified and internally inconsistent. The text says GRPO optimizes without explicit reward functions, but then defines explicit format, motion similarity, and semantic similarity rewards. It is also unclear how rewards are combined or ranked, what hyperparameters are used, and how invalid motion tokens are handled.

The motion similarity reward appears to use ground-truth paired motion during training, which makes the method closer to supervised reward shaping than the implied general RL framework. The paper does not discuss whether this limits scalability or generalization.

Reproducibility is poor. Important details are missing, including CoT prompt templates, filtering criteria, generated dataset size, tokenizer/codebook settings, SFT/RL training schedules, GRPO group size, KL coefficient, reward normalization, decoding settings, and compute budget beyond mentioning H20 GPUs.

The ablation table is difficult to interpret and does not isolate the claimed contributions cleanly. Some variants appear to use rewards without CoT or CoT without rewards, but the training setup for these variants is not explained. The textual interpretation also overstates the results.

The comparison to prior work is confusing: the text alternates between MotionAgent and MotionLLM for reference [9], and some baselines are described imprecisely. This weakens positioning and makes the main comparison less trustworthy.

The paper lacks meaningful discussion of failure cases, physical plausibility, safety/ethics, hallucinated reasoning traces, or whether generated CoT actually causally improves motion rather than merely acting as extra text supervision.

strengths: Clear and timely idea: introducing explicit action-plan reasoning and GRPO-style optimization to text-to-motion generation is well motivated, especially for compositional or long-horizon prompts.
The method is reasonably coherent: MotionCoT data generation, supervised cold start, motion tokenization, and multi-reward GRPO form a plausible end-to-end pipeline.
Quantitative results on HumanML3D are competitive with strong recent baselines, with best or near-best R-Precision@2/3, MM-Dist, Diversity, and competitive FID.
The ablation study provides useful evidence that combining CoT supervision with semantic and motion rewards improves over partial variants.
The paper includes qualitative examples for both in-distribution and out-of-distribution prompts, which helps support the claimed benefits for complex instructions.
weaknesses: The novelty is incremental rather than fundamental: the paper largely combines existing VQ motion tokenization, LLM-generated CoT supervision, and GRPO-style training, with limited new technical development beyond adapting these ingredients to motion generation.

The evaluation is not fully convincing for the strongest claims. The paper claims performance across multiple benchmarks, but the main quantitative table only shows HumanML3D; KIT-ML results are not visible in the manuscript text provided.

The out-of-distribution and compositional-generalization claims are supported mainly by qualitative examples. A dedicated quantitative OOD benchmark, human preference study, or compositional evaluation would make the central argument much stronger.

Important implementation details are underspecified, including dataset construction scale and filtering criteria for MotionCoT, GRPO hyperparameters, reward weighting/aggregation, sampling settings, training cost, and exact tokenizer/backbone setup.

The reward design may partially optimize toward standard evaluation encoders, since semantic and motion rewards use pretrained encoders from the evaluation tradition; this raises concerns about metric overfitting and whether perceived motion quality improves similarly for humans.

The ablation table is helpful but incomplete: it does not clearly isolate a strong non-CoT baseline under the same architecture/training budget, and some row configurations are hard to interpret from the table formatting.

The paper would benefit from deeper analysis of CoT quality and failure modes. Since the reasoning traces are generated by a general LLM, it is unclear how often they are physically valid, causally meaningful, or actually used by the generator rather than serving as extra text conditioning.
Reproducibility is currently limited because code/data are only promised, and many training and data-engine details appear to be deferred to supplementary material.

strengths: The paper tackles an interesting and timely problem: improving text-to-motion generation for complex, compositional prompts via explicit action decomposition and reinforcement learning alignment.

The proposed framework is conceptually clear, combining LLM-generated decomposed reasoning traces, a VQ-VAE motion tokenizer, supervised cold start, and GRPO-style RL with semantic and motion rewards.
Quantitative results are positive on HumanML3D, KIT-ML, and BABEL, with especially strong R-Precision/MM-Dist on HumanML3D and strong KIT-ML/BABEL results relative to reported baselines.
The ablation study supports that combining decomposed CoT with both semantic and motion rewards improves over using individual components.
The paper includes prompts, training hyperparameters, compute details, limitations, and an ethics statement, which improves transparency.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate. The main components are largely combinations of existing ingredients: LLM-generated plans/CoT, VQ-VAE motion tokens, standard text-motion encoders, and GRPO. The paper does not clearly establish what is technically new beyond this integration.

The evaluation is not fully convincing for a top-tier acceptance. The method optimizes rewards based on the same or closely related pretrained text-motion encoders used for standard metrics such as MM-Dist/R-Precision/FID, raising concern that improvements may partly reflect metric optimization rather than genuinely better human-perceived motion quality.

Key motivating comparisons are missing. The introduction emphasizes advantages over RL-based methods such as MotionRL and MotionCritic, but these are not included in the main quantitative tables or directly compared in annotation cost, training complexity, or efficiency.

The Decomposed CoT Data Engine is underspecified and weakly validated. The paper relies on DeepSeek-R1 to generate and filter traces but gives little detail on filtering thresholds, failure rates, dataset size after filtering, noise levels, or whether the decompositions are actually causally responsible for better motion rather than serving as additional text augmentation.

Claims about interpretability, OOD generalization, and real-world adaptability are stronger than the evidence. OOD results are mostly qualitative and limited, with no systematic compositional or long-horizon benchmark, no human study, and no physical plausibility evaluation.

Some reported conclusions are overstated. For example, HumanML3D FID is worse than several baselines, Top-1 R-Precision is tied/not best, and KIT-ML MM-Dist is worse than multiple baselines, yet the narrative repeatedly frames performance as broadly state of the art.

Reproducibility remains incomplete. Important implementation details are missing, including tokenizer architecture/hyperparameters, reward weighting or aggregation, CoT dataset statistics, decoding settings, training data splits, and whether generated reasoning traces or code will actually be released.

The ablation table has presentation and interpretation issues: several rows are hard to distinguish, the text says all ablated variants are comparable despite large drops, and there is no ablation for LLM-generated CoT quality, different backbones, reward weights, or GRPO versus simpler supervised fine-tuning.

The paper has noticeable writing and formatting issues, including grammatical errors, inconsistent capitalization, missing project page URL, and occasional imprecise terminology such as 'motionally realistic', which slightly hurts clarity and polish.

strengths: The paper tackles a relevant problem in text-to-motion generation and identifies reasonable desiderata: compositional instruction handling, semantic alignment, and reduced reliance on human preference annotation.

The proposed framework is conceptually simple and easy to understand: LLM-generated decomposed action traces are used for supervised cold start, followed by GRPO-style optimization with format, motion-similarity, and semantic-alignment rewards.
The empirical section includes multiple standard datasets, including HumanML3D, KIT-ML, and BABEL, and reports common metrics with confidence intervals over repeated evaluations.
The ablation study attempts to isolate the contributions of decomposed CoT, semantic reward, and motion reward, which is useful for understanding the method components.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. The main ingredients are standard VQ-VAE motion tokenization, LLM-generated chain-of-thought style decomposition, and RL with rewards derived from existing text-motion encoders. The paper does not convincingly establish that this combination is a substantive technical advance over prior LLM/planning-based motion generation and RL-alignment methods.

The method is under-specified in important ways. The paper does not clearly define the final combined reward, reward weights or normalization, decoding/sampling details, tokenizer/codebook settings, CoT dataset size, filtering thresholds, regeneration criteria, or the exact training data construction pipeline. This weakens reproducibility and makes the claimed simplicity difficult to assess.

There is a serious evaluation concern: the semantic and motion rewards appear to use the same or closely related pretrained encoders as the evaluation metrics for R-Precision and MM-Dist. This risks optimizing directly toward the benchmark metrics rather than demonstrating genuinely better motion generation or human-perceived quality.

The experimental evidence does not fully support the strength of the claims. On HumanML3D, Motion-R1 is not best on FID and only ties or modestly improves several metrics. Some claimed state-of-the-art statements are overstated relative to the table. The reported gains are often small, and statistical significance against strong baselines is not analyzed.

The baselines and comparisons are not sufficiently convincing for a top-tier venue. There is no careful comparison against a same-backbone LLM motion model without CoT/RL, no comparison to simply adding LLM-decomposed captions as augmented text, and no analysis separating benefits from larger backbone, data augmentation, reward optimization, and prompt formatting.

The ablation table is difficult to interpret and partly contradicts the prose. Several component combinations perform very poorly, yet the text says ablated variants achieve comparable performance. Key controls are missing, such as SFT without decomposed CoT, RL without ground-truth motion reward, different reward weights, and quality/noise analysis of generated CoT traces.

The qualitative evaluation is weak. The paper shows only a few selected visual examples and OOD prompts, with no systematic OOD benchmark, user study, physical plausibility analysis, or failure-case discussion. The claims about temporal/causal reasoning and interpretability are therefore largely anecdotal.

The paper makes strong claims about avoiding costly human annotations, but the approach still depends on ground-truth motion-caption pairs and external LLM-generated reasoning traces. The cost, reliability, and possible hallucination/noise of this automated annotation process are not quantified.

Reproducibility is insufficient for the claimed contribution. Code is only promised, not provided; implementation details are sparse; and the prompts in the appendix are not enough to reproduce the data engine, RL training, or evaluation pipeline.

The writing is generally understandable but contains overclaiming, imprecise terminology, and several grammatical/formatting issues. More importantly, the narrative repeatedly asserts improved reasoning, interpretability, and real-world applicability without enough direct evidence.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem in text-to-motion generation: improving compositional/temporal reasoning and semantic alignment for complex prompts.

The proposed combination of decomposed action-planning traces with GRPO-style reinforcement learning is technically plausible and well motivated, and the framework is relatively simple compared with preference-model-based RL approaches.

Empirical results are strong across multiple benchmarks. Motion-R1 improves retrieval metrics and MM-Dist on HumanML3D, obtains strong R-Precision and FID on KIT-ML, and reports particularly strong BABEL results.
The ablation study supports the main design choices: decomposed CoT alone is insufficient, while semantic and motion rewards are complementary and the full model performs best.
The paper includes useful implementation details, prompt templates, compute information, confidence intervals over repeated evaluations, and an explicit limitations section.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental: the work combines LLM-generated reasoning traces, a VQ-VAE motion tokenizer, and GRPO rewards, all of which are natural extensions of recent LLM/RL and text-to-motion trends.

The reward design uses pretrained text-motion encoders closely related to the evaluation metrics, raising concern that improvements may partly reflect optimization toward benchmark encoders rather than perceptual motion quality.

The Decomposed CoT Data Engine is under-specified. The paper says DeepSeek-R1 filters traces for relevance, consistency, and conciseness, but does not provide quantitative quality-control statistics, failure rates, or sensitivity to LLM-generated annotation noise.

The interpretability and reasoning claims are not directly evaluated. The paper shows qualitative examples, but does not measure whether the CoT plans are faithful, causally useful, or better than simpler caption augmentation/action decomposition baselines.
Human evaluation is missing, which is important for motion realism, semantic fidelity, and detecting artifacts that standard embedding/FID-style metrics may not capture.

Some claims are overstated. For example, the method is described as avoiding costly human annotations, but it still relies on existing annotated motion-language datasets and ground-truth motions for motion similarity rewards.
The HumanML3D gains are mixed: FID is not the best among baselines, R-Precision@1 is tied rather than clearly superior, and some improvements are modest despite strong framing as state of the art.

Reproducibility remains incomplete because code is only promised, and several practical details of tokenization, reward weighting/combination, decoding, and CoT dataset construction are not sufficiently specified for independent replication.
